articles.title: Matemático da Anthropic afirma ter provado a Hipótese de Riemann | G1
articles.standfirst: Solução teria sido possível a partir do uso do chatbot Claude, desenvolvido pela companhia. Problema não conseguia ser resolvido por matemático há mais de 160 anos.
articles.summary: Solução teria sido possível a partir do uso do chatbot Claude, desenvolvido pela companhia. Problema não conseguia ser resolvido por matemático há mais de 160 anos.
articles.body:
ChatGPT, DeepSeek, Claude, Mistral AI, Gemini, Copilot e Poe — Foto: Solen Feyissa/Unsplash

Um pesquisador da empresa de inteligência artificial Anthropic afirmou nesta sexta-feira (20) que utilizou o chatbot Claude, desenvolvido pela companhia, para demonstrar a Hipótese de Riemann, um problema que os matemáticos não conseguiram resolver em mais de 160 anos.

"Acredito que, trabalhando com o Claude, descobri uma demonstração da Hipótese de Riemann", escreveu Levent Alpoge em um documento de quatro páginas publicado em seu site.

A afirmação não foi verificada de forma independente, e a demonstração ainda não passou pela revisão de especialistas externos.

➡️Proposta pela primeira vez pelo matemático alemão Bernhard Riemann, em 1859, a hipótese aborda a distribuição dos números primos e é amplamente considerada o problema em aberto mais importante da matemática pura.

É um dos sete "Problemas do Milênio" selecionados pelo Instituto de Matemática Clay em 2000, que oferece um prêmio de um milhão de dólares (R$ 5,9 milhões) pela resolução de cada um deles.

Segundo as regras do instituto, a solução deve ser publicada em uma revista científica com revisão por pares e passar por um período de análise de dois anos.

Alpoge afirmou que o método também resolve uma versão mais ampla do problema, conhecida como Hipótese de Riemann Generalizada.

👉Ele explicou que desenvolveu, junto com Claude, uma versão da demonstração em Lean – uma linguagem de programação que permite verificar argumentos matemáticos por computador – e que, por enquanto, divulgou apenas essa versão.

Uma demonstração completa por escrito seria extremamente extensa, comentou, acrescentando que ainda não domina todos os aspectos matemáticos envolvidos e que pretende redigi-la adequadamente.

Alpoge afirmou que consultou o diretor-executivo da Anthropic, Dario Amodei, antes de anunciar o resultado.

Também reconheceu que o momento escolhido para o anúncio poderia ser recebido com ceticismo, sem dar mais detalhes, embora provavelmente estivesse se referindo à histórica abertura de capital da empresa nesta semana.

Em agosto, a Anthropic informou que uma versão do Claude, ainda não disponibilizada ao público, havia conseguido melhorar um resultado matemático relacionado à Hipótese de Riemann, mas ressaltou que não se tratava de uma demonstração completa.

A Anthropic não respondeu imediatamente a um pedido de comentários da AFP.

A afirmação surge dois meses depois que sua concorrente, OpenAI, anunciou que um modelo de inteligência artificial havia resolvido outro dos "Problemas do Milênio", relacionado às equações que descrevem o movimento dos fluidos.

Matemáticos observam que a demonstração parece correta, mas ainda não passou por uma revisão exaustiva.

Alpoge, que trabalhou em problemas relacionados à dinâmica dos fluidos com o matemático Tristan Buckmaster, da Universidade de Nova York, envolveu-se em uma disputa sobre a atribuição desse trabalho.

A OpenAI negou, na ocasião, ter agido de maneira indevida.

articles.title: Anthropic x OpenAI: como a rivalidade entre os CEOs virou símbolo da corrida pelo domínio da IA | G1
articles.standfirst: Dario Amodei deixou a OpenAI em 2020 e fundou a Anthropic com ex-colegas. Desde então, a disputa com Sam Altman envolve provocações, divergências sobre segurança e uma corrida para estrear na bolsa.
articles.summary: Dario Amodei deixou a OpenAI em 2020 e fundou a Anthropic com ex-colegas. Desde então, a disputa com Sam Altman envolve provocações, divergências sobre segurança e uma corrida para estrear na bolsa.
articles.body:
Sam Altman, CEO da Open AI, e Dario Amodei, CEO da Anthropic — Foto: Reuters/Manuel Orbegozo; Reuters/Bhawika Chhabra

A estreia da Anthropic, dona do assistente Claude, na bolsa de valores na quinta-feira (19) marcou um novo capítulo na disputa com a OpenAI , responsável pelo ChatGPT. Nos últimos meses, as duas travaram uma corrida para ver quem seria a primeira a abrir o capital.

O embate incluiu ironias e críticas, chegando ao ponto de Dario Amodei, CEO da Anthropic, e Sam Altman , da OpenAI, se recusarem a apertar as mãos durante um evento com outros executivos de gigantes de tecnologia.

A entrada da Anthropic na bolsa movimentou US$ 107 bilhões (R$ 634,6 bilhões) e se tornou a maior oferta pública inicial de ações (IPO, na sigla em inglês) da história . Durante o dia, a empresa chegou a ser avaliada em US$ 2,1 trilhões (R$ 12,4 trilhões).

🔎 Um IPO é a primeira oferta pública de ações de uma empresa. Parte do capital é vendida a investidores com o objetivo de obter recursos para ampliar operações, investir em projetos ou reduzir dívidas, por exemplo.

Inicialmente, investidores esperavam que a OpenAI entrasse primeiro na bolsa de valores, mas a Anthropic saiu à frente e anunciou, no início de junho, um pedido confidencial de IPO . A dona do ChatGPT protocolou o pedido uma semana mais tarde .

A corrida tem uma explicação simples: as duas são rivais em um mercado que exige investimentos bilionários para desenvolver modelos de inteligência artificial vez mais avançados. A disputa pela liderança também tem acirrado os ataques entre as empresas.

A rivalidade começou no final de 2020, quando Amodei, então vice-presidente de pesquisa da OpenAI, deixou a empresa com outros seis pesquisadores por divergências sobre os rumos da companhia.

No início de 2021, o grupo fundou a Anthropic com a promessa de priorizar a segurança dos sistemas de IA. O posicionamento foi visto como uma crítica à atuação de Altman à frente da OpenAI.

Em 2022, enquanto a Anthropic testava internamente a primeira versão do Claude, a OpenAI decidiu acelerar seu cronograma, que previa o lançamento do ChatGPT apenas em março de 2023.

Segundo a Reuters, Altman determinou que o ChatGPT fosse lançado o mais rápido possível. O assistente foi anunciado em 30 de novembro de 2022, enquanto o Claude veio a público cerca de quatro meses depois.

Em fevereiro, a Anthropic ironizou mudanças feitas pela concorrente em comerciais exibidos durante o Super Bowl, a final da liga de futebol americano dos Estados Unidos e o principal momento da publicidade televisiva do país.

A propaganda terminava com a frase: "Anúncios estão chegando à IA. Mas não ao Claude". Era uma referência direta à decisão da OpenAI de exibir publicidade para usuários das versões gratuitas do ChatGPT .

Sam Altman respondeu rapidamente à provocação. Ele classificou os comerciais como "engraçados", mas desonestos e disse que o ChatGPT tem mais usuários gratuitos no Texas do que o Claude em todo o território dos Estados Unidos.

Duas semanas depois, executivos de gigantes da tecnologia se encontraram na Cúpula de Impacto de IA, realizada na Índia. O primeiro-ministro indiano Narendra Modi convidou os participantes a apertarem as mãos para a foto oficial.

Mas Amodei e Altman, que estavam lado a lado, evitaram se cumprimentar , deixando ainda mais evidente a tensão entre as empresas. (veja o vídeo acima)

'Chefões' de gigantes de IA se recusam a dar as mãos em foto em grupo e evidenciam rivalidade — Foto: Reprodução/Reuters

Ainda em fevereiro, o presidente americano Donald Trump ordenou que as agências federais do país interrompessem o uso de programas da Anthropic devido às restrições impostas pela empresa ao uso de seus modelos de IA para vigilância de cidadãos e sistemas de armamento autônomos.

Dario Amodei afirmou que a companhia tinha definido um limite ético para o uso de suas ferramentas. "O uso desses sistemas para a vigilância doméstica em massa é incompatível com os valores democráticos", afirmou à época.

Após a restrição da Anthropic, o governo americano firmou um acordo com a OpenAI. Sam Altman argumentou que o contrato teria as mesmas limitações defendidas pela concorrente, mas os EUA apontaram que a IA estaria disponível para "qualquer uso legal" .

Segundo o site The Information, Amodei disse que Altman usou o entrave entre a Anthropic e os EUA para beneficiar a OpenAI. Ele afirmou que o rival trouxe "mentiras descaradas" sobre o contrato em uma tentativa de se apresentar falsamente como um "pacificador e negociador".

Em abril, a casa de Sam Altman foi atingida em um ataque com coquetel molotov. Ao comentar o caso, ele sugeriu que o discurso pessimista de concorrentes tenha aumentado a animosidade.

"Acho que a forma como a Anthropic fala sobre a OpenAI também não ajuda", disse, em entrevista ao podcast "Core Memory".

Em junho, Amodei disse à Bloomberg que deixar a OpenAI foi importante para seguir seu próprio caminho. "Por que discutir com alguém quando vocês não compartilham da mesma visão e você não confia nessa pessoa?", disse o executivo, no que foi entendido como uma referência a Altman.

Em setembro, Amodei e Altman tiveram um raro momento de concordância: a desaceleração do desenvolvimento de IA . Eles discutiram o assunto dias depois, durante uma reunião no Conselho de Segurança da ONU.

O chefe da Anthropic disse que os riscos da IA são a maior ameaça à segurança global. "Gerenciar esses riscos é maior do que só uma empresa, tem uma escala industrial e global", disse o executivo.

O CEO da OpenAI, por sua vez, defendeu transparência e cooperação internacional. "Para que a IA seja democrática, as decisões mais importantes não podem ser tomadas apenas por laboratórios em São Francisco", afirmou.

articles.title: Anthropic's 7 founders cashed out nearly $2B in record-breaking IPO | TechCrunch
articles.summary: At the upgraded $83/share IPO price, Anthropic's seven founders each pocketed $280 million, while the company nabbed nearly $105 billion.
articles.body:
Anthropic became a public company on Thursday, raising a total of $81.3 billion, including $1.95 billion for its seven founders. As we previously reported, each of them ponied up about 3.4 million shares apiece to sell in the IPO.

At the upgraded IPO price of $83 per share, that means they each pocketed about $280 million before underwriting fees and taxes. It looked like they had calculated the number of shares they planned to sell to give them each around $250 million if shares hit $74. That was the midpoint price from Anthropic’s original price range. So that’s a cool $30-ish million more for each of them than perhaps they were gunning for.

Anthropic implied in its IPO filings that the founders aren’t entirely in this for the money though. The company said that each of the founders has pledged to dedicate 80% of their personal equity in the company to philanthropy.

However, if any of them struggle to live on their quarter of a billion, they can scale back their charitable commitments. The company points out that these commitments are “voluntary, revocable expressions of each co-founder’s philanthropic intent and do not constitute legally binding obligations.”

With the IPO in the record books, there were a few other interesting numbers worth highlighting.

$104.8 billion. That’s really the amount Anthropic raised for its coffers (with a possibility of $117 billion, if the bankers buy all of their allotment of shares). In addition to selling its Class A common stock, it also sold a previously announced $26 billion worth of a special non-voting Class N stock to some of the biggest tech names in the industry.

Nvidia bought $10 billion of these Class N shares, Google bought $10 billion, and AMD, Broadcom, Micron, Microsoft, and TSMC divvied up the rest.

Just for comparison: When Facebook had its then record-breaking IPO in 2012, it raised $16 billion on IPO day.

28% stake to Amazon and Google combined. All told, at the higher IPO share price, Google wound up owning 13.4% of the company. Amazon also now has a big stake in Anthropic because when it previously invested in the AI lab as a startup, it was granted promissory notes that could be converted to equity. It converted a small percentage of them as part of the IPO, leaving it with a 14.6% stake. Had it converted all of them, Amazon could have owned nearly 24%.

The two large cloud providers now own 28% of Anthropic, the AI lab says.

More than $1 trillion. As mind-blowing as it is to raise nearly $105 billion, giving Anthropic nearly $230 billion of working capital available (along with capital it already had on hand), the company’s need for future capital is still far greater.

Anthropic needs about $70.7 billion just to cover its compute and infrastructure spending commitments in the next 12 months as of the quarter ended September 30, 2026. It needs $451.6 billion to cover these commitments before the end of 2030. And it has racked up hundreds of billions of other commitments that are either conditional (and may not happen) or haven’t been priced yet.

All told, the company has disclosed a ballpark of $1.05 trillion to $1.08 trillion in infrastructure commitments in its foreseeable future. This was a huge IPO. But it is a pricey business to run.

articles.title: Apple may be developing its own AI agent that runs your Mac | TechCrunch
articles.summary: The iPhone maker appears to be building agents that can compete with the likes of Meta Muse, Instinct, Claude, and OpenAI Dots.
articles.body:
Apple appears to be working on its own AI agent to conduct computer work on behalf of users — including using apps, accessing websites, and coding, among other things.

The news was originally reported by Bloomberg, which spotted a job listing the iPhone maker recently posted for a senior engineering manager to oversee the creation of an “AI agent that can use a computer.”

“Imagine an AI agent that can use a computer the way a capable person does,” the posting says. “It browses the web, works across apps, runs commands, writes and debugs code, and calls services, and it chooses the right tool for each step. It does all this privately and with the polish people expect from Apple.”

The posting additionally notes that the agents should be able to move “fluidly between tools” and “carry out multi-step tasks across apps, browsers, command lines, code, and APIs.”

TechCrunch reached out to Apple for more information but did not receive a response.

Agents capable of computer work have become one of the hottest commodities in the tech industry over the past year. Major labs like Anthropic and OpenAI have launched such services, while other major tech brands — like Meta, which recently launched its Muse agent line — have also moved into the space. It makes sense that Apple — which is trying to expand its AI offerings in the new John Ternus era — would want to follow suit.

Bloomberg additionally notes that, at the same time that Apple is working on its own digital assistant, the company is making it significantly harder for third-party agents to gain total control over its computers.

The outlet notes that the version of its upcoming macOS 27.3 will deploy warnings discouraging users from granting full access to third-party agents. In October, Apple issued a notification to developers stating that the company planned to “introduce additional controls to ensure that users who genuinely wish to grant an app this extraordinary level of access can only do so with very explicit user action.”

Bloomberg writes that while the iPhone maker “has eyed introducing the service as soon as the end of next year,” progress on its in-house agent “remains in the early stages.”

articles.title: As Anthropic makes its Wall Street debut, CEO Dario Amodei says ‘We will not bend to either business or political pressure’
articles.summary: Claude-maker Anthropic made its blockbuster debut on Wall Street with the company’s valuation reaching nearly $2 trillion.
articles.body: Claude-maker Anthropic made its blockbuster debut on Wall Street with the company’s valuation reaching nearly $2 trillion. Shares of the company closed at $97.17, up by 17% from its IPO price of $83. Soon after the debut, Anthropic shared a statement from CEO Dario Amodei reaffirming the company’s core focus on safety, committing to pace AI training and deployment as needed to maintain human control while resisting business or political pressures, framing this as essential to avoid risks like misuse or loss of control. “Today puts the company in a stronger financial position, and in doing so only strengthens our resolve to do the right thing,” Amodei said.“If we can show it’s possible to make the right choices on safety and still build an incredibly successful company, others in our industry will be inspired to do the same. We call this a race to the top,” he added.Here’s what CEO Dario Amodei said on Anthropic IPO"My co-founders and I started Anthropic because we believe that the most powerful technology of our time should be built for the benefit of humankind.Daniela and I lost our father to a disease that, just a few years later, became curable. I started my career in biology, hoping to help future cures come sooner. In the lab, I saw the vast thicket of complexity that scientists face when they’re trying to understand disease and develop new treatments.So many of the scientific tools that can cut through that thicket—tools for gene editing, gene synthesis, controlling brain cells with light—started as pure ideas. In other words, they came from thinking. From intelligence.Human intelligence has already made diseases like plague, smallpox, and polio history for most of the world. But progress on other diseases has been too slow for so many patients and their families. Going from a great idea to a treatment can take decades: it took many years from the first discovery of a strange repeating pattern in DNA to the approval of the first treatment for a disease using CRISPR.Nature is full of these patterns. But we’ve had too little intelligence to decipher most of them; too few scientists, with too little time. Now we can build that intelligence. Whether it’s protein folding, drug design, cancer genetics, or clinical trial administration, scientists across many areas of biology and medicine are finding Claude can help them do their research in a fraction of the time it would’ve taken just a couple of years ago. I believe sufficiently powerful AI, working in concert with humans, could compress a century of scientific and medical progress into a decade.I don’t want to get ahead of myself. At this point all we have are early results. Experiments and clinical trials will still take time. And although they involve slow and ponderous processes, I believe those processes can be substantially accelerated by AI. We hope that in the future fewer families miss a cure by just a few years.Medicine is just a particularly vivid example, but there are many others. Our customers—the world’s most ambitious companies, nonprofits, and individual people—are already applying the intelligence we’ve built to stimulate economic growth; lift people out of poverty; protect democracy and free societies; even make everyday services like the DMV work better. We’re proud to work alongside them. And I’m extremely optimistic about what we can do together in the future.At the same time, we have always been honest that this technology has very real risks. These range from misuse of the technology by individuals or nation-states, to economic disruption, to losing control of AI systems. We discuss these risks not because we think they are inevitable, but because we think they are avoidable.Avoiding them depends on the choices made by the people building AI. There is a gigantic difference between how AI will go if we pay little attention to safety, versus how it will go if we are obsessed with safety. And an obsession with safety and with public benefit has been woven into Anthropic’s DNA from the start. From safeguards against biological and cyber risks, to alignment training and testing, to looking inside our models like an X-ray, Anthropic has pioneered methods for understanding and steering the behavior of AI systems.There is much work still to be done, and the most difficult safety work lies ahead of us. The incredible talent of the company that has enabled us to build the most capable AI systems will need to be directed, even more so than it has already, towards double- and triple-checking that those AI systems are safe and secure.And to state it unequivocally, we will pace the training and deployment of AI systems, taking as long as is necessary to have confidence that they are safe and will remain under human control. We will not bend to either business or political pressure. Today puts the company in a stronger financial position, and in doing so only strengthens our resolve to do the right thing.If we can show it’s possible to make the right choices on safety and still build an incredibly successful company, others in our industry will be inspired to do the same. We call this a race to the top. When the race to the top is working properly, it doesn’t matter which company has the best models—everyone wins because everyone is building safely. The race to the top works best when driven from the front of the pack, and we fully hope and expect to do so, but the goal is to make the whole industry better, regardless of whether Anthropic is winning or losing at any given time.The advent of machine intelligence is one of the seminal moments in human history, and we have a rare opportunity to shape it for the better.This moment is bigger than any one company, or any one country. It will take all of us, working together, to ensure this technology goes well for us and the many generations to come. Starting today, we hope that you’ll join us on this mission."Fearless legend or grounded realist? Rate yourself on 11 categories in the Great Indian Confidence Survey – find out in 3–6 min

articles.summary: Cambridge University recently named ‘human’ as the Word of the Year 2026, a choice that caught the attention of Microsoft founder Bill Gates.
articles.body: Cambridge University recently named ‘human’ as the Word of the Year 2026, a choice that caught the attention of Microsoft founder Bill Gates. Reacting to the Cambridge University announcement, Bill Gates said he believes AI has the potential to cure diseases, improve education and give people more time for what matters most. However, he also stressed the need to make deliberate choices about how AI fits into our lives and where humans should remain at the centre. “Cambridge Dictionary just picked “human” as its Word of the Year. The measure of AI’s success should be how much it improves lives, so I can’t think of a better choice for this moment,” Gates wrote in an X post.“I believe AI has the potential to cure diseases, improve education, and give people more time to spend on the things that matter most. But we need to make deliberate choices about how it fits into our lives, including where we want people to remain at the center,” he further stated.Why Cambridge Dictionary named ‘human’ as word of the year 2026Explaining its selection, it said:“The year was defined by global debates on what it means to be human when AI is blurring the boundaries between people and machines.In 2016, many public figures defended humans and humanity in the age of AI. Bill Gates made the case for “human reserved jobs”, such as caregivers, that should never be taken by machines, in a widely read essay.Throughout history, the adjective human has signified people, as opposed to animals and gods (and, more recently, machines). Increasingly seen in compounds such as human-written, human-generated, and human-made, it now also denotes that something is created by or typical of people as opposed to AI .It’s possible that this shift is simply a natural linguistic development, reflecting the ubiquity of AI, but it could be evidence of something more interesting: a turning point in our attitude towards artificial intelligence.When we look back on 2026 in years to come, it might prove to have been a pivotal moment in the story of human versus machine. In May of this year, the University of California, San Diego, published a landmark study which for the first time revealed empirical evidence for artificial intelligence systems passing the Turing Test. In 73 percent of cases, after a 15-minute text conversation, GPT-4.5 was judged to be ‘human’.We have now reached a point where AI can produce writing, art, and music that can pass for human-made content. Some people are even questioning whether AI has achieved sentience. This gives rise to some profound existential questions. What are the implications for humanity? articles.title: Signal is blocking Gemini and Siri AI from reading your screen
articles.summary: Signal is restricting the ability to take screenshots on Android and iOS devices in an effort to prevent AI agents from reading users’ messages and other data.
articles.body: Signal is restricting the ability to take screenshots on Android and iOS devices in an effort to prevent AI agents from reading users’ messages and other data. The agentic AI capabilities built into operating systems that analyze on-screen information to learn more about the user are “undermining Signal’s ability to independently guarantee privacy,” Signal president Meredith Whittaker said in a blog post, while urging OS providers to make it easier for app developers to control what data agents can access. “We want to be very clear: it is a serious problem that Signal – and application developers beyond – lack robust tools to prevent AI agents from undermining application-level privacy,” Whittaker said. “Even where we are able to detect and block AI data access, Google, Apple, Microsoft, and others do not provide ways for developers to easily restrict such AI data access without making drastic compromises to the core user experience. This is also the reason we are currently unable to implement these protections on macOS.” Signal is addressing the privacy concerns by blocking the ability to take screenshots in the app on iOS 27 and Android, which should prevent Siri, Gemini, and other Android AI assistants from reading on-screen content. Users can restore screenshot capabilities in Signal’s app settings, but Whittaker warns that doing so will “potentially expose your (and your contacts’) Signal content to these AI agents, and break our privacy guarantees.” Whittaker admits that Signal’s screenshot blocking remedy is “incomplete,” as it doesn’t address alternative ways that AI agents can access app data, such as retrieving it via the device filesystem. [Image: Signal’s app security settings on Android devices will display this message for the screenshot blocking feature. Signal took a similar approach last year to prevent Microsoft’s controversial Recall feature from capturing secured chats. The encrypted messaging service says it’s struggling to develop a better solution due to the lack of available information regarding how AI agents are actually accessing application data, and is now calling on Apple, Google, and Microsoft to provide “simple technical tools and accurate documentation” to app developers. Signal also says more tools are needed to prevent third-party agents, like Meta’s Muse, from using deep accessibility settings in apps like a “skeleton key” to access application data. “We all need to recognize that the current integration of AI agents into the operating system, without these common-sense remedies, represents an existential threat to privacy at the application layer, and the ability of independent developers like Signal to protect your sensitive data,” said Whittaker. “Signal is the canary in the coal mine, but this affects the entire ecosystem and should galvanize anyone who cares about these fundamental rights.”

articles.title: Democrats weaponized AI fears for political gain, and it worked
articles.summary: Recent events may be a harbinger of things to come; no one knows. What we do know is that fear-mongering about AI became a political weapon for Democrats, independent of sober consideration of its merits or risks.
articles.body:
What an astonishing split screen! Many Americans, alarmed by an unusual series of nationwide software outages , are prepping for an AI catastrophe , even as investors charge into Anthropic’s history-making IPO , driving the AI giant’s market capitalization to a breathtaking $2 trillion.

It’s hard to imagine two more disparate messages arriving at the same moment. How could the country be so divided on the outlook for the greatest technology development in a generation?

Like everything splitting our country in two today, politics has played a role. Many smart people, including some in the industry , have voiced concerns about the fast-evolving models developed by Anthropic, Open AI and others — fears of bots crushing employment, causing a new pandemic or taking over from humans have been purposefully amplified by China-allied activists and by Democrats. But it has also been well documented that groups sympathetic to Beijing have sowed anxiety about AI and data centers, leading to efforts to slow the industry’s necessary build-out of computing power.

China is desperate to win the AI race ; blocking the expansion of U.S. data centers helps its cause.

Some communities are genuinely alarmed about data centers driving up electricity bills or leading to potential water shortages. But the widespread opposition has been totally out of proportion to the risks or costs. Polling now shows that Americans would rather live next door to a nuclear power plant than a data center , which is absurd. Politicians can and should alleviate computing campus burdens by requiring developers to generate their own power and minimize water usage.

But rather than adopt common-sense policies, Democrats chose to weaponize the issue. We know why. Thanks to Joe Biden’s unwelcome regulatory zeal, Big Tech began to shift its support to Republicans and to President Trump. CEOs like Tim Cook, Sam Altman, Elon Musk and Sundar Pichai attended Trump’s inauguration in 2025 , and donated money to his campaign or inauguration fund. Meta’s Mark Zuckerberg gave a million dollars to the fund and claimed he was “very keen to play an active role” in the “president’s tech policymaking,” according to Business Insider. Amazon founder Jeff Bezos also gave a million to the inauguration, after The Washington Post helpfully declined to endorse a presidential candidate for the first time in decades.

Democrats, threatened by the torrent of money Big Tech could throw into campaigns, began screaming about “oligarchs” taking over the country; the battle lines were drawn. Breitbart presciently predicted earlier this year that ahead of the midterms, “Americans should expect a torrent of messaging designed to heighten anxiety over real and perceived AI job losses, a plan left-leaning globalist billionaires hope will sour voters’ economic outlook and help Democrats return to power.” Spot on.

Connecticut’s progressive Sen. Chris Murphy was just one of many Democrats living up to that expectation, telling the Bulwark last December , “There is going to be a growing appetite from voters to support candidates that are going to help them manage the potential coming disaster as AI poisons our kids and destroys all of our jobs.”

Earlier this year, Sen. Bernie Sanders (I-Vt.) wrote a letter to AI executives asking them to stop pursuing new models. “It is not too late to avoid disaster,” he wrote, citing reports that AI could “lead to new bioweapons that result in the deaths of tens of millions of people.” He joined forces with Rep. Greg Casar (D-Texas) in September to introduce legislation that would “ban the creation of systems that humanity cannot fully control” and writing of “potential deadly consequences.”

For months, Democrats campaigned on a platform of doom and alarmism. They warned that AI was going to gut the job market and could lead to all-out catastrophe. And it worked.

Polling showed Americans becoming more worried about AI’s impact on their lives, with an increasing number thinking the technology could do “more harm than good.” Democrats rode a tidal wave of anxiety to an historic midterm victory.

But their fear-mongering has left Americans frightened about the future.

Events over the last two weeks have heightened those fears. The FAA’s nationwide ground stop and outages at Microsoft, Apple, the NSA, JP Morgan Chase and United Airlines — variously described as “glitches” or “bugs” — have unsettled the country. U.S. authorities and CEOs have issued reasonable explanations for the purportedly unconnected events, but even those answers raise questions.

We are told that AI systems are uncovering software vulnerabilities at lightening speed, and that companies and institutions are responding in kind, frantically trying to patch those flaws. It makes perfect sense that such triage could lead to temporary interruptions; we have all experienced hiccups following software updates on our cellphones or TVs. But the very fact that hackers are now armed with super-capable bots that can help them invade and wreck important systems is not comforting.

Recent events may be a harbinger of things to come; no one knows. What we do know is that fear-mongering about AI became a political weapon for Democrats, independent of sober consideration of its merits or risks.

What we also know is that AI brings the promise of extraordinary benefits in curing diseases, facilitating entrepreneurship, improving business productivity and supplementing the labor that is lost as Boomers retire.

Democrats, ever opportunistic, will moderate their antagonism to AI as tech leaders shift their allegiances (and campaign donations) back to those newly in power, and as officials welcome the revenues that data centers can offer. Count on it.

Liz Peek is a former partner of major bracket Wall Street firm Wertheim and Company.

articles.title: Anthropic mathematician claims to have solved prestigious Millennium Prize problem with Claude
articles.summary: Anthropic mathematician Levent Alpöge claims to have proved the Riemann hypothesis, one of the Millennium Prize problems in math.
articles.body: Anthropic mathematician Levent Alpöge claims he has proved the Riemann hypothesis, one of mathematics’s most notoriously difficult problems, with the help of Claude, cracking a puzzle that has eluded some of the world’s best mathematicians for decades. If verified, it would mark yet another seismic achievement for AI in mathematics and add to the upheaval already unleashed by OpenAI’s previous, often inelegant forays into the field. Alpöge’s solution has yet to be verified independently. Anthropic has not commented or involved itself in Alpöge’s announcement. In a document on his website, Alpöge says he texted Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei about the solution “late Sunday night” and suggests he held off publication until after the company’s IPO on Thursday. The Riemann hypothesis is one of seven Millennium Prize problems, which are widely considered some of the most formidable open challenges in mathematics. First proposed in 1859, the Riemann hypothesis concerns the distribution of prime numbers and how zeroes of a function are involved. It’s regarded as one of the most important unsolved problems in mathematics. A statement on Alpöge’s website says Claude was integral to developing the proof: > I believe I have, working with Claude, discovered a proof1 of the Riemann Hypothesis. In fact, the method easily extends much further, resolving the so-called Generalized Riemann Hypothesis, and I expect, with more time, the Extended Riemann Hypothesis too. Claude and I have also formalized the arguments without assumptions. It is natural to feel that this is an end, in my case a loss of a principal guiding light, but what I saw during the course of progress so amazed me that I believe it is one dawn across science of something far greater. The Verge reached out to Anthropic but didn’t immediately hear back. Anthropic said it was working on the Riemann Hypothesis with Claude in August, but noted at the time: “We don’t expect that the techniques Claude used will lead to proving the Riemann hypothesis.” Alpöge’s solution, presented in Lean, has only been published on his website and has not yet been publicly accepted by the Clay Mathematics Institute, which administers the Millennium Prize and offers a $1 million bounty for each problem solved. Under the institute’s rules, a proposed solution must be published and withstand at least two years of scrutiny before it can be considered for the prize, during which time it must have “received general acceptance in the global mathematics community.” In the quarter-century since the prize was established, only one problem has been officially solved: The Poincaré conjecture, a topological problem concerning three-dimensional spheres. In September, OpenAI claimed to have cracked another, the Navier-Stokes problem, which concerns the flow of fluids. OpenAI said it pursued Navier-Stokes after hearing rumors that rival researchers were closing in on a solution. Alpöge had been working on the problem with New York University mathematics professor Tristan Buckmaster. Buckmaster claimed OpenAI produced a solution for Navier-Stokes using the route he and Alpöge were working on with OpenAI’s Codex and Claude. OpenAI spent millions of dollars and deployed 10,000 agents in the attempt. The result is widely considered credible, though it has yet to receive formal recognition. But the achievement has been marred by allegations of questionable research practices, including claims it used unpublished work from mathematicians who had shared their research with its AI tools. OpenAI has strongly denied wrongdoing, but this has done little to quell the uproar. Though most of the spotlight has been on OpenAI’s movement in math, Alpöge said in July that he solved the Jacobean conjecture using Claude. The deluge of findings has left mathematicians scrambling to digest the material and figure out where they belong in what is rapidly becoming a profoundly different mathematical landscape.

articles.title: AI claimed a solution to the 167-year-old Riemann Hypothesis — and a human did, too | TechCrunch
articles.summary: Mathematicians are having their minds blown by the latest AI-driven result — and there's a competing human solution, too.
articles.body:
It’s a big week for Levent Alpöge: The mathematician saw his employer, Anthropic, become the first publicly traded frontier AI lab. He also appears to have solved one of the most important problems in mathematics.

“The precise timing is horrible,” he wrote in an essay announcing his findings and describing how he messaged Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei last Sunday night to ask how to announce that he had found a Lean-compilable solution to the Riemann Hypothesis, which dates back to 1859 and is among the Millennium Prize math problems.

The Hypothesis conjectures that there is a hidden structure underlying the appearance of prime numbers. If the claimed result holds true, we’re entering sublime-mysteries-of-the-universe territory.

Maybe the best way to understand how exciting this is to the mathematics community is to watch the experts puzzling through the result in a chat on Zulip . Mathematicians like Chris Birkbeck, a number theorist at the University of East Anglia, are posting thoughts like this …

The cohomology bound is proved by what looks like an automorphy-lifting argument. It genuinely uses the existence of Galois representations attached to regular algebraic, polarized cuspidal automorphic representations of GL_n over CM fields, along with base change, Jacquet–Shalika, Clozel’s purity, Bernstein–Zelevinsky, the main theorem of CM, Deligne–Ribet and more.

For my part, I tapped out of mathematics at college calculus, so I can’t help decode exactly what that means.

But that comment was followed by 20 readers reacting 🤯.

It will be a while before the mathematics community feels like it has a handle on the proof, but most appear confident that the formalized Lean result will hold. Lean is an an open source language that essentially helps verify mathematical proofs.

Alpöge appeared in his essay to feel a bit guilty about releasing the proof without a truly human-intelligible explanation, but his obsession with the problem since childhood made him feel he “could not live” if he waited to release the finding.

Alpöge described a “stream-of-consciousness jaunt through the experience of finding all the pieces of the argument through incredible confusion with Claude” with more than a hint of AI euphoria, describing how the model “flew, and danced, and sparkled near that finish line.”

However, for all that action to mean anything, we’ll have to wait for humans to be able to understand the result and explain it to each other, something Alpöge has committed to pursue.

Alpöge and a collaborator, NYU mathematician Tristan Buckmaster, also released another important proof related to the Navier-Stokes equations, problems that helped kick off the race between frontier labs and mathematicians to solve outstanding problems this summer.

Meanwhile, Ravi Vakil, a Stanford professor and the president of the American Mathematics Association, posted a proof of the General Riemann Hypothesis written by Stanford postdoc Alessandro Masullo, noting that “it is all human, with no AI. The hope was to bring Alessandro to Stanford for a year to polish the writing and then announce it after running it by enough people. Now it seems best to put out the current draft.”

In a brief introduction to his proof, which he said is the result of 12 years of work, Masullo wrote that “if any message at all this work is meant to send to the mathematician who feels discouraged by the pace and tone of the current climate, it is this: we are still here. We are very much alive. We are not going anywhere.”

articles.title: Cognition in Talks for $75 Billion Value With New Funding
articles.summary: Artificial intelligence coding startup Cognition AI Inc. is in funding talks at a $75 billion valuation, just two months after announcing its most recent fun...
articles.body:
(Bloomberg) -- Artificial intelligence coding startup Cognition AI Inc. is in funding talks at a $75 billion valuation, just two months after announcing its most recent funding round, according to people familiar with the matter.

The company is considering raising $2 billion or more in the financing, the people said, asking not to be identified discussing private information.

The efforts are ongoing and details could change, the people said. If completed, the financing would be Cognition's third this year. It's already raised over $3 billion in 2026 so far, including over $2 billion at a $48 billion value in September.

Cognition didn't respond to requests for comment. Business Insider reported in October that Cognition was weighing a new fundraising effort.

The startup has surged this year as investors have piled into companies building AI agents for software development. Cognition and its flagship product, AI engineering agent Devin, compete with the likes of Cursor, which SpaceX acquired earlier this year for $60 billion. Several major Cursor backers, including Andreessen Horowitz and Accel, invested in Cognition after that acquisition closed.

articles.title: Anthropic may have solved major maths problem Reimann hypothesis
articles.summary: A mathematician at Anthropic says he used an AI to prove the famed Riemann hypothesis, though verification will take some time.
articles.body:
An Anthropic employee and mathematician claims to have used the company's artificial intelligence (AI) chatbot to prove the famed Riemann hypothesis.

Levent Alpöge said on Friday, a day after Anthropic made its US stock market debut , that over the course of about six weeks, he used the Claude chatbot to create a detailed proof of the maths problem.

If found to be correct, the proof would be among the most significant in history. Alpöge described it as "one dawn across science of something far greater".

The claim comes as AI firms like OpenAI have in recent months announced scores of solutions to major higher maths problems that have eluded scholars for decades.

As for the Riemann hypothesis proof put forward on Friday, it was found using a non-public version of Anthropic's Claude.

It is a nearly 170-year-old maths problem that deals with prime numbers and is widely considered to be the single most famous problem in maths, in large part due to how complex it is.

Named for the mathematician Bernhard Riemann, the hypothesis puts forward that prime numbers have a determined order along the number line.

Prime numbers are the bedrock of higher maths, leaving breakthroughs related to them to have broad impact.

Alpöge said that he messaged Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei on Sunday, asking him directly about how he could announce the discovery.

"The precise timing is horrible," Alpöge said, referring to Anthropic's public stock listing. "If I could have, I'd have finished this all much earlier."

"I am clearly unilaterally responsible for feeling I just could not live if I waited even longer. There is an obvious cynical view, to do with the timing, but it is false," he added.

The complete textual proof that Alpöge put forward in Lean, a computer language used for confirming maths proofs, is over 250,000 pages long.

Terrance Tao, a prominent mathematician, said on Friday that verification of the proof is still some way off.

"I imagine the digestion process will take some time, though in this case at least we have a human author to communicate with to assist with this task," Tao said.

No such human was obviously a part of major maths proofs made earlier this year using AI.

OpenAI in September claimed that employees using a non-public version of its AI tools were able to solve part of a notoriously difficult problem in just 88 hours. The problem was part of the Navier-Stokes equations, which concern how fluids move.

More than 10,000 AI agents, or computer programmed bots that operate somewhat autonomously, were put to the task as an AI training exercise.

The proof that OpenAI released on Navier-Stokes has yet to be confirmed as accurate, and it set off criticism within academic and higher maths communities and organisations about the use of AI to solve maths problems.

Anthropic has also claimed to have made other progress and solutions in maths and physics .

A group of maths scholars said AI companies boasting of major solutions to show how sophisticated their commercial products had become was "detrimental to the science of mathematics".

"We are witnessing a general threat to intellectual work, with misalignment between the outcome of the use of AI and its initial purpose," the scholars said in a group letter.

A month later, OpenAI released what it claimed were solutions, proofs, or major progress on 372 more outstanding higher maths problems.

It will take months, if not longer, for those claims to be reviewed by experts to prove their validity.

articles.title: Black Friday 2026: Can ChatGPT and other AI tools find you the best bargains?
articles.summary: We put four AI models to the test to see if they could save us money on a new TV.
articles.body:
Whether it's scrolling through endless choice, spotting fake reviews, or working out if a "deal" is a deal at all, Black Friday sums up a lot of online woes.

Retailers promise bargains - but the sheer number of offers can leave us feeling no closer to finding the best deal.

It's an area where generative AI products, such as ChatGPT, Claude and Gemini, have promised to help.

But are they any good at finding Black Friday deals? We had a go ourselves a week ahead of the big day.

Figures suggest relatively few UK shoppers currently go to AI tools for help.

A recent YouGov survey of 19 countries found the UK ranked second-last in the proportion of people who said they had used AI to help them shop.

Crucially, 36% of respondents who said they would be shopping around Black Friday didn't plan to use an AI tool at all.

But the survey suggested a growing number of people were considering it - and tech firms have released features to capitalise on this.

Amazon launched Alexa for Shopping for UK users in November and OpenAI launched a Shopping Research tool on ChatGPT days before last year's Black Friday.

In the US, Google recently launched Universal Cart, with AI-powered features such as price tracking and identification of relevant promo codes.

But there has been criticism that fact-checking AI ends up taking more time, while some brands are working to try to make sure their products show up in chatbot answers.

We asked four models to find a 55-inch TV deal, using the free versions of many of the most popular tools.

While this was not a rigorous scientific test, the experience we had produced mixed results.

ChatGPT - full price and not available to buy

OpenAI's ChatGPT came up with four options.

Its top pick was a Hisense TV on Chinese retailer Joybuy's website, on sale for £499 down from £649.

The next recommendation was a 55-inch TCL-branded TV, but a sidebar showed prices for the 50-inch version, from £379 to £814.

Option three was the same Hisense TV as before, but for full price at £649 from John Lewis and Richer Sounds.

This was the "best safer purchase" according to ChatGPT, as the sites offered longer guarantee periods.

But clicking on the links did not go well. Both retailers said the TV was no longer listed online.

The fourth option was equally fruitless - another TCL TV, at full price, £150 over our budget and not available online.

At the bottom, ChatGPT served one last offer - "one OLED option to compare" - for a £1,100 LG TV that was marked as "Ad" .

Claude produced the shortest answer of all the models we tested, and unlike the others, it did not give much detail on the specifications of each model.

Instead, it seemed to base its results on a small number of reviews published online.

It recommended the same two TCL TVs as ChatGPT.

But when we clicked on the links, they sent us to two dead pages on the Richer Sounds website.

Some other links led to year-old round-ups of Black Friday 2025 deals.

Claude was not very enthusiastic about its other two recommendations due to a lack of independent reviews - calling one "a decent option" but saying it "wouldn't pick" the other.

It also listed two Samsung TVs, but it told us not to buy them, with one "over budget and not clearly better than the TCLs".

We were left wondering why it even mentioned them in the first place.

Different AI model, same TV manufacturers - albeit different Hisense and TCL models to the previous chatbots' recommendations.

Gemini generated a table comparing four different models, but offered no links to the stores it named, so we searched for them ourselves.

The prices for one TCL TV were correct at £649, but it was sold out at one of the named retailers.

It said the other TCL model was available from Argos and Currys for £539 - correct for Argos, but when we checked Currys, it was £60 more expensive.

Again, it included two Samsung models to avoid due to lower screen specs.

Alexa came back with four TVs, from its own Amazon Ember at £532 to a £699 Samsung.

But its top recommendation was to go for another Samsung model at £616 (down from £749), based on its picture quality and Amazon customer rating.

Its fourth option was for a Sony TV, but it was only 50 inches, leaving us unsure why it had included it.

All the prices stated were correct, but Amazon only searches its own store. Alexa did acknowledge this, encouraging us to check its rivals for better deals, "as prices can vary" and we could get longer guarantees elsewhere.

There are methods that can boost the likelihood of getting a better response, from crafting more informative prompts to upping a chatbot's "thinking" level.

Tech journalist Alex Hughes had better luck than we did when he used ChatGPT's agentic AI mode to find a TV in last year's Black Friday sales.

Agentic AI is still in its early days, but it allows AI to act with more autonomy and carry out multi-step tasks.

The search took about 20 minutes "with very little work on my end needed," Hughes wrote for Tom's Guide in November 2025.

A year on, he told the BBC he didn't go through with buying a TV at that time.

He did later purchase one of the seven models ChatGPT had surfaced - but he had found it for a lower price in a bricks-and-mortar shop.

Will he be using AI to find Black Friday deals again this year? "Probably not," he said.

He reckoned it saved him time, but "when you're trying to deal with something like live price data... it will be inconsistent and quite often incorrect".

While we were served up the same brands again and again, in reality there are tonnes of products listed for sale around Black Friday.

Naureen Mohammed, who advises businesses on how to get their products to appear in AI results, told the BBC customers did not see the full picture when they talked to chatbots.

If businesses fail to update their prices when people start hunting for bargains, "last year's prices are served up as today's deals".

"I suspect the whole model for advertising is going to start influencing AI recommendations," she said.

Her own analysis of chatbots' Black Friday tech deals in the UK suggested the big retailers came out on top - with Amazon mentioned in half of responses, and Currys following closely behind.

Her tips include asking an assistant "is that this year's price?" and clicking on the links provided - "because you shouldn't take any advice from the AI system at face value".

But consumer group Which? recently said inaccurate pricing in AI results added more work to Black Friday deal-hunting.

"If you ask ChatGPT for a list of 10 laptops under £400 and seven of the results are priced higher, you've likely wasted a good chunk of time going through them to discover the bot gave you only three options," said senior researcher Hannah Walsh.

"The opposite is also true - you could miss out on great models in your budget if ChatGPT tells you they are more expensive than they actually are."

articles.body: A few days ahead of Anthropic’s $1.4 trillion initial public offering (IPO), company CEO Dario Amodei sat down with JPMorgan CEO Jamie Dimon to explain the strict hiring philosophy that has kept the artificial intelligence (AI) company unified – even when it means turning away brilliant engineers. According to Amodei, prioritising company culture over raw technical ability has been a non-negotiable rule since the very beginning. Amodei explained that when he and his six co-founders left their previous company to launch Anthropic, they made an agreement on day one to put talent and culture first – a priority so central that Amodei still spends much of his own time on it.“From day one, myself and the other six co-founders said, ‘we're going to focus on talent, and we're going to focus on culture. And right from the beginning, we set things up in such a way that we have a culture interview that everyone goes through, and we've been very disciplined about turning down people who are deeply technically talented, but who don’t fit our culture,” Amodei told Dimon.Who Anthropic refuses to hireTo protect how its teams work together, Anthropic enforces clear boundaries during its mandatory culture interviews. Amodei explained that the company actively screens out candidates who fall into three specific categories: “Jerks, spotlight-stealers and those who have no indifference to public benefit”. He admitted that passing up top technical talent hurts in the short run. However, he emphasised that sticking to those standards consistently pays off by creating a workplace where everyone is on the same side.“We don't want people who are jerks. We don't want people who try to steal the show and don't work well with others. We don’t want people who aren’t oriented towards the public benefit, and it turns out if you stick to that consistently, it's painful in the short run, but you get a team where everyone works together, and everyone is on the same side,” the Anthropic CEO explained.“One of the things that most causes difficulty for companies is if you have an incredible team, but people aren't working together, they're working against each other, you have this team that works against that team that works against the third team, and they spend all of their energy fighting each other,” he added.Notably, all 7 co-founders are still at the company, and two senior product people quit and came back within two weeks.Fearless legend or grounded realist? articles.title: Americans don’t have to choose between our AI future and ripping off copyright owners
articles.summary: The DOJ's embrace of fair use for AI training breaks with the White House's own framework, as OpenAI, Microsoft and news groups battle over copyright.
articles.body: One of the biggest court battles over artificial intelligence (AI) is putting an age-old legal principle to the test — and raising important questions about the Trump administration's AI policy. Several news organizations, including The New York Times, are suing OpenAI and Microsoft for using millions of newspaper articles to train AI systems. The newspapers argue that the tech firms violated basic copyright protections. The tech firms contend that training their models on those articles qualifies as "fair use," a longstanding principle that allows copyrighted material to be used in certain ways without permission from or compensation to the copyright owner. The Department of Justice (DOJ) has sided squarely with OpenAI's position — breaking with the administration's previously more balanced stance on the issue. The DOJ filed a statement of interest embracing an extreme vision of fair use that would grant AI companies virtually unfettered access to copyrighted material for commercial training, without obtaining permission from or compensating the creators whose works fuel these systems. MIKE DAVIS: THE TRUMP DOJ SHOULD WITHDRAW ITS STATEMENT OF INTEREST IN THE OPENAI LAWSUIT This expansive interpretation threatens to turn a narrow copyright exception into a blanket exemption for the world's most powerful and profitable industries. The DOJ's reasoning is that requiring a copyright license for material used in AI training would impose high costs on AI developers. It claims those costs could make it harder for small companies to compete and hamper U.S. AI leadership and national security. FOX NEWS POLL: VOTERS SEE AI REGULATION AS URGENT, RANK SAFEGUARDS AHEAD OF INNOVATION Those concerns deserve consideration. But the DOJ's aggressive arguments in the brief depart from more measured guidance elsewhere in the administration. The White House's official AI framework acknowledges valid arguments on both sides of the copyright debate. Likewise, the Carolina Principles for Emerging Technologies, adopted by G20 ministers at the Commerce Department's recent Innovation Ministerial, recognize that the intersection of AI and copyright poses "complex legal and policy questions." The principles note the "essential role" of copyright protections in supporting creators and call for respecting IP as a pillar of G20 AI policy. MUSIC INDUSTRY FENDS OFF FLOOD OF AI MUSIC 'STEALING' THE CHARTS The DOJ statement also overlooks how its stance could favor larger AI companies over smaller firms and startups. Several AI startups have argued that paying for the material they use provides more reliable access to training material, reduces legal uncertainty and improves models. Other companies have emerged to aggregate copyrights and make licensing easier. It's particularly problematic for large AI companies to complain about paying for access to copyrighted materials. They are among the best positioned to pay for those materials, and doing so would help develop the kind of licensing markets they claim are lacking. OBAMA CRITICIZES TRUMP ON APPROACH TO AI, ESCALATES WARNING FOR STRONGER REGULATION And even if national security were a legitimate justification, the government could not simply disregard property rights. The Constitution and other laws require just compensation when private property is taken for public use, and intellectual property rights are still property rights. Letting AI firms appropriate creators' IP without permission or compensation would be akin to letting data center builders seize private land without paying fair value. If courts adopt the DOJ's position that fair use protects AI developers in virtually all circumstances, it would reduce incentives to create new works. Copyrights encourage creative work by assuring writers, artists and other creators that their work can't be easily stolen or copied. Licensing those rights allows creators to earn a living and underpins over $1 trillion in U.S. economic activity. Weaker copyrights could result in fewer human-created books, articles, research papers, films and songs. Ironically, that could eventually leave AI systems with fewer and lower-quality materials to train on – a scenario that serves no one's interests. All of this is why the Trump administration would be wise to follow its own AI framework and let the court system evaluate AI copyright disputes case by case, rather than arguing for unfettered fair use exceptions. The DOJ's reasoning is that requiring a copyright license for material used in AI training would impose high costs on AI developers. It claims those costs could make it harder for small companies to compete and hamper U.S. AI leadership and national security. Policymakers also have a role to play. One promising bill is the bipartisan CLEAR Act. Introduced in February by California Democrat Sen. Adam Schiff and Utah Republican Sen. John Curtis, the CLEAR Act would require AI developers to publicly disclose the copyrighted works used in each new generative-AI model's training dataset. The proposal would not settle whether any particular training practice qualifies as fair use. But it would give creators more information about whether their work helped train an AI system, enabling them to pursue appropriate compensation or other remedies when they believe their rights have been violated. Rather than treating licensing as an obstacle to innovation, policymakers should foster a market where AI developers can efficiently license copyrighted material while respecting creators' rights.
